title: The Exchange, Both Ways
description: Contact connected ecosystems separated for thousands of years: crops, animals, and diseases flowed in both directions, with growth on one side and catastrophe on the other.
essential_question: Why did the same exchange produce growth and catastrophe at once?
learning_objectives: List the major crops, animals, and diseases that crossed the Atlantic in each direction.
Explain how American crops supported population growth in Afro-Eurasia.
Use causation and comparison to weigh the exchange's unequal effects.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
Rapid population growth in Afro-Eurasia supported in part by calorie-rich American crops.
Outbreaks of Afro-Eurasian diseases that caused catastrophic Indigenous mortality in the Americas.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [solemn]The potato is from Peru. Corn is from Mexico. The horse came from Spain, the pig from Europe, and smallpox came from ten thousand years of crowded cities. [beat] For most of human history, none of them had ever met. Then, in [date:1492], the ocean between them closed. What crossed it fed millions on one side of the Atlantic, and killed millions on the other. The same ships. Both ways. [beat] Historians call it the Columbian Exchange.

narration.text: Start with what sailed east, toward Europe. Maize, corn, the grain that had fed Mexico for thousands of years. The potato, dug from the Andes. Tomatoes, sweet potatoes, cacao, and tobacco. [beat] None of it existed in Europe. No Italian had ever tasted a tomato. No Irishman had ever seen a potato. Within a century, maize and tomatoes spread across southern Europe. The potato took longer. [beat] A Spanish observer, seeing these strange harvests for the first time, wrote home about them.

narration.text: Westward sailed a different cargo. Wheat, sugarcane, bananas. And animals Europe took for granted: horses, pigs, cattle, goats, chickens. [beat] The Americas had never seen any of them. Within decades, pigs were running wild in the forests, cattle were spreading across the grasslands, and the horse reached the Plains, where it turned hunters into the continent's great mounted powers.

narration.text: [solemn]And then the deadliest cargo. Smallpox, measles, influenza. Epidemic diseases born in the crowded cities and livestock pens of Afro-Eurasia, carried across the ocean in European bodies. [beat] Native peoples had no resistance. Whole villages died in weeks. Remember this: the main cause of the die-off was disease, not warfare. [beat] Even sickness traveled east. Sailors may even have carried syphilis back to Europe. The exchange went both ways, down to the germs.

narration.text: Now the question that matters. [beat] Look at this potato. Plain, ugly, dug from the dirt. Why did this root help feed a continent? [2s pause] Because it cheated. A field of potatoes could feed three times as many people as a field of wheat. And potatoes grew where wheat could not: ground too wet, too dry, too poor. [beat] Europe's peasants had always lived one bad harvest from hunger. The potato gave them a backup.

narration.text: Maize did the same work across southern Europe and Africa. Together, American crops saved millions in Afro-Eurasia from starvation, and the world's population rose after 1500. That population boom runs on American calories. [beat] More food, more people. That is the whole mechanism, and the exam will ask you for it.

narration.text: So weigh it. The same ships carried both. Afro-Eurasia got the calories: potatoes, maize, foods that fed millions. The Americas got the germs: smallpox, measles, death on a scale warfare never reached. [beat] Look at this engraving. A sugar mill in the Americas, printed in Europe around 1600. Sugar: grown by African labor, on American land, for European profit. Three continents in one picture.

narration.text: [beat]Why unequal? The two sides brought different things to the contact. Afro-Eurasia brought diseases born of crowded cities and livestock. The Americas brought crops that fed millions. [beat] Same ships, same ocean. Growth on one side, catastrophe on the other. That asymmetry is the whole lesson.
